title: PRD: Status page transparency upgrades (component granularity + incident templates + post-incident summaries)
creator: Marissa Cole
description:
## Summary
Customers increasingly use our public status page to make real-time decisions (retry/backoff, fallback models, region pinning, Dedicated failover). Today, our page is too coarse (e.g., “API Degraded” when only Streaming is affected), updates vary by oncall, and post-incident follow-ups are inconsistent.

This PRD defines product requirements for:
1) **More granular, customer-comprehensible status components** (by capability + deployment mode + region where appropriate)
2) **Standardized incident update templates and cadence guidance** (Investigating → Identified → Monitoring → Resolved)
3) **Consistent customer-facing post-incident summaries** aligned with internal postmortems while respecting disclosure boundaries
4) **Workflow/tooling assist** so comms are timely and not overly manual

This is a cross-functional reliability/comms upgrade, but this PRD is the product spec for what we ship externally and how we measure adoption/quality.

---

## Background / Problem
### What’s happening
- Platform surface area has expanded (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private; multiple regions; multiple model families; streaming/tool calling).
- Enterprise customers expect clarity during partial degradation ("what exactly is broken?") and expect written follow-ups.

### Pain points
- **Ambiguous impact**: Customers can’t tell whether failures are limited to Streaming, a specific model family, a region, or the Console.
- **Update quality variance**: Updates sometimes lack either (a) impact, (b) mitigation/workaround, or (c) next update time.
- **Support load**: Support receives repeated “Is it just us?” and “Which region/models?” questions during incidents.
- **Post-incident inconsistency**: Some incidents get follow-up summaries; others do not, causing churn/renewal risk.

### Evidence / signals
- Support escalations citing coarse components and missing regional specificity (see SUP-18421, SUP-18502).
- Enterprise asks about comms practices during security reviews and procurement (AE email thread + sales calls).

---

## Goals
1) Customers can answer within 60 seconds:
   - “What’s impacted?” (capability + region + deployment mode)
   - “How bad is it?” (degraded vs partial outage vs outage, in customer language)
   - “What should I do?” (retry/backoff, fallback models, region pinning, contact Support)
   - “When will you update next?”
2) Reduce incident-related Support back-and-forth by providing actionable, consistent status updates.
3) Publish post-incident summaries for major incidents with a clear SLA and consistent format.
4) Make it easy for oncall/SRE to do the right thing via templates + light workflow enforcement.

---

## Non-goals
- Overhauling our internal incident response process (roles/severity definitions) beyond what’s needed for external comms.
- Publishing sensitive details (customer names, exploit details, provider contractual details, vulnerability-like specifics).
- Guaranteeing customer-specific RCA writeups on the public status page (those remain through Support/CS channels when appropriate).

---

## Personas
### 1) Customer engineer / oncall (Hosted API)
Needs: quick, accurate impact + workaround to keep production stable.

### 2) Enterprise platform lead (Dedicated / Private)
Needs: clarity on whether issue is in Redwood control plane, serving plane, region capacity, or their Private deployment; needs follow-up summary for internal reporting.

### 3) Support/CS
Needs: status updates that answer the top customer questions and can be copied into macros without rewriting.

### 4) Redwood SRE / Incident Commander
Needs: fast path to publish high-quality updates while actively mitigating.

---

## User stories
### Customer-facing
- As a customer engineer, when streaming responses fail but non-streaming requests succeed, I want the status page to reflect **Streaming degraded** (not generic API) so I can decide to disable streaming or switch to non-streaming temporarily.
- As a customer running workloads in eu-west, I want to know if the incident is **region-scoped** so I can route to a different region.
- As an enterprise customer, after a Sev1+ incident, I want a **post-incident summary** with timeline, impact, and prevention actions within a predictable timeframe.

### Support/CS
- As Support, I want status page updates to include a **customer action** section so I can send guidance quickly (retry/backoff, fallback model family, region pinning, expected symptoms).
- As CS, I want a stable summary format so I can attach it to renewal risk notes and customer QBRs.

### SRE / Oncall
- As Incident Commander, I want a template-driven update flow that prompts me for (impact, mitigation, next update time) so updates are complete.
- As SRE, I want component selection rules that prevent under/over-scoping (“mark API down” vs “Streaming degraded”) and support multi-component incidents.

---

## Proposed customer-facing component model (v1)
We will present customer-comprehensible components, organized primarily by capability + deployment mode.

### Hosted API (global and/or regional where applicable)
- **API Gateway** (auth, request routing, rate limiting, 4xx/5xx at edge)
- **Text Generation** (non-streaming generation endpoints)
- **Streaming** (SSE/websocket streaming responses, disconnects, keepalive)
- **Embeddings**
- **Rerank**
- **Capacity & Routing** (queueing, elevated 429s, autoscaling lag, model routing/fallback behavior)

### Console
- **Redwood Console** (dashboards, usage analytics, rollouts UI, auth)

### Dedicated
- **Dedicated Control Plane** (cluster management, scaling operations, config rollouts)
- **Dedicated Serving** (request serving in dedicated pools; may be region- or cluster-scoped when meaningful)

### Private
- **Private Control Plane** (orchestration, upgrades, policy)
- **Private Serving** (if we can detect broad impacts without exposing customer-specific infra)

### Region scoping
For Hosted API serving, we will support **regional sub-components** (us-east, us-west, eu-west) where it helps customers route traffic.

Principle: default to the most specific component(s) that accurately represent impact, without leaking internal service names.

---

## Functional requirements

### FR1: Component granularity & naming
- Provide a finalized taxonomy of public components (names + definitions + examples of partial impact).
- Ensure components are:
  - understandable to customers (avoid internal jargon like “scheduler”, “orchestrator”)
  - stable over time (avoid frequent renames)
  - mappable from internal alerts/services with high confidence

Acceptance criteria:
- Updated status page shows new components with no broken historical incident pages.
- Internal mapping guidance exists and is referenced in oncall runbooks.

### FR2: Incident update templates (phase-based)
Create copy-ready templates for:
- Investigating
- Identified
- Monitoring
- Resolved

Each template must include prompted fields:
- **Impact** (who is affected, what symptoms)
- **Components** (one or more; region when known)
- **Mitigation / Workaround** (what customers can do now)
- **Next update time** (timestamp, not vague “soon”)
- Optional: “What we’re doing” (brief, non-sensitive)

Acceptance criteria:
- Templates are adopted in oncall workflow for Sev1+ incidents.
- Updates cannot be published empty/low-information (guardrail enforcement defined in ENG work).

### FR3: Update cadence guidance (by severity)
- Sev0/Sev1: first update target + minimum cadence (e.g., every 30–60 minutes while investigating/mitigating, with flexibility).
- Sev2: less frequent but still predictable.
- Guidance for long-running degradations: keep “next update time” moving, even if no new info.

Acceptance criteria:
- Documented cadence rules and an escalation path if updates are overdue.

### FR4: Post-incident summaries
- For Sev0/Sev1 incidents, publish a customer-facing summary within **3 business days** (SLA) unless blocked by security/legal.
- Standard format:
  - What happened (one paragraph)
  - Customer impact (duration, affected components/regions, request failure modes)
  - Timeline (start, detection, mitigation, resolution; customer-visible times)
  - Root cause category (customer-safe category; avoid exploit-level detail)
  - Mitigations + prevention (what changed / what will change)

Acceptance criteria:
- Summary template exists with a redaction checklist.
- Workflow creates a summary stub and reminders to the owner.

### FR5: Disclosure & approvals
- Define who can publish externally and when to involve Security/Legal.
- Define “never disclose” items (vulnerability-like detail, customer names, sensitive provider constraints, etc.).

Acceptance criteria:
- Written approval policy exists and is referenced in the status update workflow.

### FR6: Tooling assistance (non-optional for adoption)
- Incident workflow should nudge oncall to:
  - pick correct components
  - use correct phase template
  - include next update time
  - draft updates synced to incident state transitions (draft-first, then publish)

Acceptance criteria:
- Minimal additional burden during incident response (goal: <2 minutes to create an update draft).

---

## UX / Content requirements
- Customer language must be:
  - specific about symptoms (e.g., “streaming responses may terminate early”)
  - honest about uncertainty (“We’re investigating elevated disconnects; root cause not yet confirmed”)
  - actionable (“retry with exponential backoff; consider disabling streaming; pin to us-west”)
- Avoid internal service names; use component names and customer-facing product terms.

---

## Metrics / Success criteria
### Primary
- **Time to first status update** for Sev1+ (target improvement; measured from incident declare → first public update).
- **Update completeness**: % of updates including impact + mitigation/workaround + next update time.
- **Support escalation rate** during incidents: reduction in incident-related “what’s impacted?” tickets.
- **Post-incident summary SLA compliance** for Sev1+.

### Secondary
- Customer feedback (CSAT during incidents, qualitative enterprise feedback).
- Internal: reduced manual work / fewer comms rewrites by Support.

Instrumentation needs (owned by Eng/SRE): tagging incidents by status component; dashboards for cadence and SLA compliance.

---

## Rollout plan
### Phase 1: Pilot (1 region/service group)
- Enable new component taxonomy for Hosted API in one region (proposed: us-east).
- Use templates + cadence guidance for Sev1+ incidents only.
- Validate:
  - mapping correctness
  - update workflow speed
  - customer comprehension (Support feedback)

### Phase 2: Expand (all Hosted API regions + Console)
- Add remaining regions and capabilities.
- Add Console component updates.

### Phase 3: Dedicated + Private components
- Add components relevant to Dedicated control plane/serving.
- Define what we can/should publish for Private without exposing customer-specific details.

### Phase 4: Backfill/migration
- Ensure old components map/alias to new taxonomy without breaking historical incident pages.

External comms:
- Update docs: “How to read our status page” and “What to expect during incidents”.
- Optional: short status page announcement when rollout completes.

---

---

## Risks & mitigations
- Risk: Over-scoping incidents (too many components marked degraded) → Mitigation: mapping guidelines + examples + reviewer/approval path for Sev0.
- Risk: Under-scoping incidents (missing region/component) → Mitigation: improved signals + "unknown scope" language allowed, with follow-up.
- Risk: Slower oncall response due to comms overhead → Mitigation: draft-sync tooling + templates with prompts.
- Risk: Disclosure issues → Mitigation: strict policy + Security/Legal escalation path.

---

## Open questions
1) Exact list of Hosted API regional components: always-on vs only when incident occurs?
2) For model-family-specific incidents, do we expose “Model family: X” as a component or only mention in incident text?
3) For Private incidents: what qualifies as a platform-wide impact we can publish publicly vs customer-specific issue routed through Support?
4) Do we want a public “Incident history RSS / webhook” improvement as follow-on scope?

---

## Acceptance criteria (for PRD sign-off)
- Stakeholder alignment: SRE sponsor + Support lead + Security approver sign off on taxonomy + templates + post-incident summary format.
- Engineering has clear, testable requirements for:
  - component creation/migration
  - workflow prompts/guardrails
  - summary workflow and reminders
  - metricing for timeliness and compliance

Owner: Paula Mendes
Approvers: Sean Gallagher (SRE), Dev Patel (Support Ops), Dr. Aisha Rahman (Security/Disclosure), Marissa Cole (Product)
comments: 2024-06-21 (Sean Gallagher): Strong +1 on regional scoping. We should default to global components unless there is a clear customer action (re-route to us-west). Suggest we explicitly call out when we *don’t yet know* whether scope is regional.

2024-06-24 (Dev Patel): Please include explicit customer guidance snippets for the common cases: 429s/capacity, streaming disconnects, elevated latency. Support macros can then link to the status incident + copy the action text verbatim.

2024-06-26 (Dr. Aisha Rahman): Post-incident summaries are fine, but root cause must remain category-level. Avoid timelines that reveal sensitive internal detection gaps or vulnerability-like exploitation paths. Add “never disclose” bullets to the template.

2024-06-28 (Marissa Cole): Let’s ensure component names don’t encode internal architecture. Prefer “Capacity & Routing” over “Scheduler”. Also ensure Console is separate; enterprise customers treat Console outages differently than serving outages.

2024-07-03 (Rafael Mendes): From SRE side, templates need to be short enough to use under pressure. Suggest guided prompts in incident-bot + guardrails requiring next-update time. Otherwise adoption will be inconsistent.
2024-07-05 (Paula Mendes): Incorporated feedback. Marking PRD as Done and linking to ENG epic + DES naming review. Next step is Confluence publication + training rollout.
